references.text: Job compares his inner state to new wine in sealed wineskins that are about to burst—the same image of new wine bursting old containers.
Joshua 9:17 mentions wineskins with wine (neḥōt yayin), illustrating the common practice of storing wine in skins in biblical times.
The parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus uses the same image of new wine in old wineskins to illustrate that the new he brings cannot be forced into old religious forms.
The parallel passage in Mark where Jesus says that no one puts new wine into old wineskins, or else the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the skins are lost.
The preceding parable about no one tearing a piece from a new garment to patch an old one—the same principle that the new and the old cannot be mixed.
The following verse gives the conclusion: new wine must be put into fresh wineskins, and whoever has drunk old wine does not want new—expanding on the point in verse 37.

Paul writes that if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation—the old has passed away, behold, the new has come. This reflects the theological principle in Jesus' parable that new life requires new forms.
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the new covenant that makes the first one obsolete—the new cannot be contained within the old system, corresponding to Jesus' image of new wine in old wineskins.
